# Saṅgāmāvacarajātaka (Ja 182)

**ID:** Ja 182
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** At Home in Battle

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Saṅgāmāvacarajātaka* (Ja 182), titled *At Home in Battle* in English, opens with the verse line “O Elephant, a hero thou” and is framed as a teaching delivered by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana concerning the Elder Nanda [SuttaCentral]. The narrative relates to Nanda, the Buddha’s half-brother or younger brother, who joined the Saṅgha but remained tormented by longing for his former bride or lady [Swanson 2004; Pye, Skillful Means]. As a pedagogical device, the Buddha took Nanda to heaven and showed him five hundred celestial nymphs, promising that he could win them by persevering in the ascetic life [Pye, Skillful Means]. This episode is notably cited in *Jātaka* No. 478 as an exemplum of the Buddha’s deployment of skillful means (*upāya*) [Pye, Skillful Means].

Nanda’s struggle with desire and his subsequent training forms one of the most prominent hagiographical narratives across early and classical Buddhist literature [Donner 1976; Swanson 2004; Bass 2013]. In the Pāli tradition, parallel treatments of the story appear in the *Udāna* (Ud 3.2), while the broader northern and Sanskrit literary traditions preserve versions in Aśvaghoṣa’s *Saundarananda*, Kṣemendra’s *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā*, and the *Ta chih tu lun* [Donner 1976; Swanson 2004; Bass 2013]. SuttaCentral records four translations of this jātaka across four languages [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus detects no direct Pāli-internal text reuse and finds no cross-language matches meeting its threshold [DharmaNexus].
